```{r, include = FALSE}
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>"

```

```{r setup, message=FALSE}
library(fixedincome)
```

Every interest rate calculation needs a period of time: a rate is compounded
*for* some time, and a curve has a rate *at* each maturity.
In `fixedincome` this period of time is a `Term` object.

## What is a Term

A `Term` is a number with a unit. The units can be `"day"`, `"month"` or
`"year"`, and the plural forms are also accepted.

```{r}
t <- term(6, "months")
t
```

`Term` extends `numeric`, so it is a vector: it has a length, it can be
indexed and it can be used as a column of a `data.frame`.

```{r}
terms <- term(c(1, 21, 42, 63), "days")
length(terms)
terms[2:3]
data.frame(terms = terms, rate = c(0.1365, 0.1366, 0.1368, 0.1371))
```

The units are kept in the `units` slot, and `as.numeric()` returns the value
without the units.

```{r}
t@units
as.numeric(t)
```

When the units are not given, days are used.

```{r}
term(10)
```

## Creating Terms

There are three ways to create a `Term`.

From a number and its units, with `term()`.
Each element can have its own units.

```{r}
term(1:3, "years")
term(c(10, 6), c("days", "months"))
```

From text, with `as.term()`.

```{r}
as.term(c("6 months", "1 year", "21 days"))
```

From two dates and a calendar, with `term()`.
This creates a `DateRangeTerm`, a `Term` in days that also keeps the two dates
and the calendar used to count the days between them.
The days are counted with the [bizdays](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=bizdays)
package, so with the `"Brazil/ANBIMA"` calendar only business days are
counted.

```{r}
d1 <- as.Date("2022-12-23")
d2 <- as.Date("2023-01-03")
term(d1, d2, "Brazil/ANBIMA")
term(d1, d2, "actual")
```

## Converting units

How many days are there in one year? It depends on the market convention:
252 business days in Brazil, 360 or 365 actual days elsewhere.
This convention is the daycount, so converting a `Term` from one unit to
another needs a daycount. This is done with `todays()`, `tomonths()` and
`toyears()`.

```{r}
one_year <- term(1, "year")
todays(daycount("business/252"), one_year)
todays(daycount("actual/360"), one_year)
todays(daycount("actual/365"), one_year)
```

```{r}
toyears(daycount("business/252"), term(126, "days"))
tomonths(daycount("business/252"), term(63, "days"))
```

A month is one twelfth of a year, so with `business/252` one month has
21 days.

## Operations

### Terms and numbers

Arithmetic with a number keeps the `Term` and its units, and comparison with
a number returns a logical.

```{r}
t <- term(c(10, 20), "days")
t * 2
t + 1
t > 15
```

### Terms and Terms

Arithmetic and comparison between two Terms work when both have the same
units:

- `+`, `-` and `%%` return a `Term`;
- `/` and `%/%` return a number, because the units cancel out;
- comparisons return a logical.

```{r}
t1 <- term(42, "days")
t2 <- term(21, "days")
t1 - t2
t1 / t2
t1 > t2
```

`*` and `^` between two Terms are not defined, because days times days has
no meaning as a period of time.

```{r}
try(t1 * t2)
```

### Terms with different units

Terms with different units can't be combined directly.
To add one month and twelve days, the month must first be converted into days,
and that needs a daycount.
So these operations raise an error.

```{r}
try(term(1, "month") + term(12, "days"))
```

Convert first, then operate.

```{r}
todays(daycount("business/252"), term(1, "month")) + term(12, "days")
```

### Other functions

`c()` combines Terms, and each element keeps its own units.

```{r}
c(term(1, "day"), term(5, "days"))
c(term(10, "days"), term(6, "months"))
```

`diff()` returns the Terms between consecutive elements, and `shift()` moves
the elements, filling the gap with `NA`.

```{r}
terms <- term(c(1, 21, 42, 63), "days")
diff(terms)
shift(terms)
```

Summary functions like `sum()` and `cumsum()` return plain numbers.
Use `term()` to get a `Term` back.

```{r}
term(cumsum(terms), "days")
```

## Terms with interest rates

A spot rate is compounded for a `Term`.
The units of the `Term` are converted with the daycount of the rate, so six
months and half a year give the same compounding factor.

```{r}
sr <- spotrate(0.1375, "discrete", "business/252", "Brazil/ANBIMA")
compound(sr, term(6, "months"))
compound(sr, term(0.5, "years"))
compound(sr, term(126, "days"))
```

The terms of a `SpotRateCurve` are kept in days.
Indexing a curve with `[[` accepts a `Term` in any units, and converts it to
days with the daycount of the curve.

```{r}
curve <- spotratecurve(
  c(0.1315, 0.1319, 0.1338, 0.1348, 0.1372, 0.1381),
  c(1, 21, 42, 63, 126, 252),
  "discrete", "business/252", "Brazil/ANBIMA",
  refdate = as.Date("2022-08-05")
)
curve[[term(1, "year")]]
curve[[term(c(3, 6), "months")]]
```

With an interpolation, the curve also returns rates between its terms.

```{r}
interpolation(curve) <- interp_flatforward()
curve[[term(c(10, 100), "days")]]
```

Forward rates between two Terms are computed with `forwardrate()`.

```{r}
forwardrate(curve, term(3, "months"), term(6, "months"))
```
